summaryTr: Seoul Mayor Oh Se-hoon acquitted on appeal in opinion poll bribery allegations
Appellate court recognizes reasonable doubt due to lack of key evidence
Ruling and opposition parties should cease political attacks and focus on Seoul's livelihood policies
editorial.bodyTr: Seoul Mayor Oh Se-hoon has been acquitted on appeal in a case involving allegations of contracting polls on someone else's behalf. The appeals court determined that the key evidence rested solely on the testimony of Myung Tae-gyun and that the allegations had not been proven beyond reasonable doubt. Rather than engaging in political disputes between ruling and opposition parties over the acquittal, both sides should focus their efforts on policy competition for the livelihood of Seoul residents.

editorials.titleTr: Conservative Party Lays Foundation for Praising Yushin Dictatorship Under Guise of Academic Debate
summaryTr: A ruling party lawmaker held a forum at the National Assembly glorifying Yushin authoritarianism.
Park Chung-hee was hailed as a democratization contributor, whitewashing the regime's historical wrongs as achievements.

editorials.bodyTr: A senior People Power Party lawmaker held a forum at the National Assembly together with a New Right-affiliated organization that glorified Yushin dictatorship. At the forum, former President Park Chung-hee was elevated to the status of a democratization contributor, while his wrongs such as suppression of democracy were reframed as achievements. Following the previous controversy over a discussion session demeaning May 18, the party's failure to apply the brakes has heightened concerns that historical perception is drifting toward extremes.

editorials.titleTr: Over 110,000 Vulnerable Servers Exposed to 'Bugmageddon' — Emergency Response Underway
summaryTr: Critical PHP Vulnerability Discovered, 110,000 Domestic Servers at Risk
Spreading Amid Millions of Attack Attempts Worldwide
Government Must Conduct Full Investigation and Establish Interagency Measures
editorials.bodyTr: A serious vulnerability enabling remote command execution has been discovered in PHP, widely used globally, with an estimated 110,000 vulnerable servers identified domestically. Although PHP developers deployed a security update on the 21st, attack attempts have surged to millions, prompting several countries to suspend website operations in response. Domestically, the crisis alert level has been raised to caution, but given the significant risk posed by the prevalence of outdated versions and high usage rates, the government must conduct a comprehensive audit and reorganize inter-ministerial countermeasures.

The court panel determined that the credibility of Myung's statement, the sole evidence, was low.

The acquittal has reignited controversy over the investigative methods employed by Special Counsel Min Jung-gi and allegations of political bias.

editorial.titleTr: Editorial: As North Korea Escalates Threats, Seoul Hesitates on Proportional Response While Allied Coordination Falters
summaryTr: North Korea condemns warning shots as provocation, threatens to resume loudspeaker broadcasts toward the South and deploy new countermeasures
Decision on reciprocal measures delayed due to disagreement within the government; effective response measures must be developed
North Korea escalates threats amid instability in the South Korea-U.S. alliance; restoring alliance trust is urgent
editorial.bodyTr: Kim Yo-jong, head of the North Korean Workers' Party's General Affairs Department, denounced our military's warning shots at the Military Demarcation Line as provocation in a statement yesterday. She threatened to resume loudspeaker broadcasts toward the South and place new countermeasures along the entire border on standby. The day before, Kim Yo-jong visited the MDL and announced plans to resume loudspeaker operations targeting the South in October. North Korea, which has denied responsibility despite three of our soldiers being wounded by landmines planted in the Demilitarized Zone, is raising the level of threats by taking issue with our military's justifiable warning. Kim Yo-jong also hurled abusive language such as "fool" and "idiot" at South Korean officials. The fact that North Korea has issued eight statements over the past twenty days, including this latest statement, suggests an intent to test our government's response and stoke internal discord in the South. The Defense Ministry announced it would take proportional measures against North Korea's provocation, but has failed to clearly spell out specific response plans. Reactivating loudspeaker broadcasts toward the North could be considered a corresponding measure, but the Defense Ministry and military authorities appear reluctant to make a quick decision given that the previous removal of loudspeaker facilities and halt of broadcasts in June last year symbolized the Lee Jae-myung administration's conciliatory North Korea policy. Moreover, with the Unification Ministry expressing opposition, there remains no consensus within our government. Nevertheless, it is reasonable for us to prepare effective countermeasures, including reactivating loudspeaker broadcasts, in preparation for the possibility of North Korea resuming broadcasts toward the South. We cannot allow unilateral conciliatory measures to fail in gaining North Korea's reciprocal response while constraining only our own options. With tensions rising near the MDL due to North Korea's provocative threats, the government must establish concrete response principles on how to address the situation by stages. Additionally, the government should strengthen coordination with the United Nations Command to hold North Korea strictly accountable for its violations of the armistice agreement. As North Korea's threat level continues to escalate, it is deeply concerning that the South Korea-U.S. coordination, which forms the foundation of deterrence against the North, is not proceeding smoothly. U.S. Ambassador to Korea Michele Steel has described current South Korea-U.S. relations as experiencing "turbulence." The government must not take lightly the signs of friction in the continuing alliance and should make restoring trust in the alliance its urgent priority.

editorial.title: The employment divide
editorial.body: Record wage disparities show structural barriers to stable jobs for younger workers A labor market can add jobs while closing off the kind of work that allows people to build secure lives. South Korea illustrates this paradox. Of the 113,000 additional wage earners recorded over the past year, 91.2 percent entered non-regular positions. In August, non-regular workers numbered a record 8.67 million, up 103,000 from a year earlier. They accounted for 38.5 percent of all wage earners, the highest share since the current statistical method began in 2003, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics. Non-regular workers, many in part-time or temporary roles, earned an average of 2.11 million won ($1,589) a month from June through August, compared with 4.05 million won for regular employees. The resulting monthly pay gap of 1.94 million won was also a record. These figures describe a labor market expanding at its margins while offering too few paths into its protected core. The wage gap, however, needs careful interpretation. Monthly earnings do not account for differences in hours worked, and part-time roles make up a growing share of non-regular employment. Excluding part-time workers narrows the gap to 954,000 won. Even on this basis, a substantial disparity remains, pointing to disadvantages beyond shorter working hours. The shift also reflects Korea’s aging population. The number of non-regular workers aged 60 and older rose by 135,000, exceeding the overall increase of 103,000 as numbers fell in other age groups. Many work in health and social welfare, where non-regular employment grew by 112,000 over the year. Such jobs provide income and meet genuine care needs, but their expansion cannot compensate for a labor market in which younger workers struggle to establish lasting careers. The consequences can persist long after a first job ends. A study tracking 2,000 people born from 1989 to 1998 found that those who began in regular employment spent an average of eight years and three months in regular, full-time work over the following decade. Those who started in non-regular jobs accumulated just three years and two months. The difference in time spent unemployed was also two years. An insecure start can shape a working life for years to come. Employers have their own reasons to favor flexibility. At Korea’s five major banks, regular staffing fell by 4,080 between the end of 2022 and July 2026, while the non-regular headcount rose by 1,048. Digitization and branch closures have reduced demand for some conventional roles, giving banks further incentives to contain labor costs. Yet replacing experienced employees with a shifting pool of contractors can weaken institutional memory and make oversight harder. Payroll savings can come at the cost of service quality and internal controls. The government plans to publish a roadmap by year-end for equal pay for work of equal value. Beginning in 2027, it also plans to pay a “fairness allowance” to short-term public-sector contract workers upon departure. The aim of closing unjustified pay gaps is laudable. But a mandate alone cannot erase the incentives created by a system in which dismissal is difficult and wages often rise automatically with seniority. Employers may respond by slowing recruitment or outsourcing more work. Younger workers could end up bearing the cost of reforms intended to help them. Pay should reflect the work performed rather than years spent in a post, with employers given reasonable room to reorganize and workers protected by portable social benefits when jobs end. A labor market that protects those already inside while restricting entry for everyone else will struggle to turn economic growth into broad-based opportunity. Equal pay will remain an empty promise if access to secure employment continues to narrow. 임금 격차 사상 최고 기록, 청년층의 안정적 일자리 진입에 구조적 장벽

노동시장은 일자리를 늘리면서도 사람들이 안정적인 삶을 영위할 수 있는 종류의 일을 제한할 수 있다. 한국은 이러한 모순을 보여준다. 지난 1년간 추가로 기록된 임금근로자 113,000명 중 91.2%가 비정규직에 진입했다. 8월 비정규직 근로자는 사상 최고인 867만 명으로, 1년 전보다 103,000명 증가했다. 이는 전체 임금근로자의 38.5%를 차지하며, 현 통계 방식이 시작된 2003년 이후 가장 높은 비중이다. 통계청에 따르면 비정규직 근로자의 대다수는 시간제나 임시직으로 일하며, 6월부터 8월까지 평균 월 211만 원을 벌었다. 정규직 근로자의 평균 월급은 405만 원이었다. 월급 격차 194만 원도 사상 최고치를 기록했다. 이러한 수치들은 주변부에서만 확대되면서 보호받는 핵심 부분으로 진입할 수 있는 경로가 너무 적은 노동시장의 모습을 보여준다. 다만 임금 격차는 신중하게 해석해야 한다. 월별 소득은 근무 시간의 차이를 반영하지 않으며, 시간제 일자리가 비정규직 고용에서 차지하는 비중이 점점 커지고 있다. 시간제 근로자를 제외하면 격차는 95만 4,000원으로 줄어든다. 이 기준으로도 상당한 격차가 남아 있으며, 이는 단순히 근무 시간이 짧은 것 이상의 불리함을 시사한다.

이러한 변화는 한국의 고령화를 반영한다. 60세 이상 비정규직 근로자는 135,000명 증가했으며, 이는 다른 연령층에서 감소하면서 전체 증가분인 103,000명을 초과했다. 많은 사람들이 보건·사회복지 분야에서 일하고 있으며, 이 분야에서 비정규직 고용은 지난 1년간 112,000명 증가했다. 이러한 일자리는 소득을 제공하고 실질적인 돌봄 수요를 충족하지만, 이 분야의 확대만으로는 청년층이 지속 가능한 경력을 구축하기 어려운 노동시장을 보완할 수 없다. 그 결과는 첫 번째 일자리가 끝난 이후에도 오래 지속될 수 있다. 1989년부터 1998년 사이에 태어난 2,000명을 추적한 연구에 따르면, 정규직으로 시작한 사람들은 그 이후 10년 동안 평균 8년 3개월간 정규직 전일제 일을 했다. 비정규직으로 시작한 사람들은 3년 2개월만 정규직에 있었다. 실직 기간의 차이도 2년에 달했다. 불안정한 시작은 수년 동안 일생의 경력을 좌우할 수 있다.

고용주들도 유연성을 선호할 자신들의 이유가 있다. 한국의 5대 은행에서는 2022년 말과 2026년 7월 사이에 정규직 인원이 4,080명 감소한 반면 비정규직은 1,048명 증가했다. 디지털화와 지점 폐쇄로 인해 기존 업무의 수요가 줄어들었고, 이는 은행들에게 인건비를 억제할 추가적인 동기를 제공했다. 그러나 경험 많은 직원을 유동적인 계약직 풀로 대체하는 것은 조직의 기억력을 약화시키고 감시를 더 어렵게 만들 수 있다. 급여 절감은 서비스 품질과 내부 통제의 악화로 이어질 수 있다.

정부는 연말까지 동일 가치 노동에 대한 동일 임금에 관한 로드맵을 발표할 계획이다. 2027년부터는 단기 공공부문 계약직 근로자에게 퇴직 시 "공정성 수당"을 지급할 계획이다. 정당하지 않은 임금 격차를 줄이려는 목표는 바람직하다. 그러나 해고가 어렵고 임금이 종종 근속연수에 따라 자동으로 상승하는 체계가 만드는 인센티브를 명령만으로 없앨 수는 없다. 고용주들은 채용을 줄이거나 더 많은 일을 외주화함으로써 대응할 수 있다. 청년층이 자신들을 돕기 위한 개혁의 대가를 치르게 될 수도 있다.

임금은 직무 경력보다는 수행한 업무를 반영해야 하며, 고용주에게는 조직을 재편할 합리적인 여지를 주고 근로자들을 일자리가 끝날 때 이동식 사회보장제도로 보호해야 한다. 이미 고용된 사람들을 보호하면서 다른 모든 사람들의 진입을 제한하는 노동시장은 경제 성장을 광범위한 기회로 전환하는 데 어려움을 겪을 것이다. 안정적인 일자리에 대한 접근이 계속 좁혀진다면 동일 임금은 공허한 약속으로 남을 것이다.

editorials.title: The employment divide
editorials.body: Record wage disparities show structural barriers to stable jobs for younger workers A labor market can add jobs while closing off the kind of work that allows people to build secure lives. South Korea illustrates this paradox. Of the 113,000 additional wage earners recorded over the past year, 91.2 percent entered non-regular positions. In August, non-regular workers numbered a record 8.67 million, up 103,000 from a year earlier. They accounted for 38.5 percent of all wage earners, the highest share since the current statistical method began in 2003, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics. Non-regular workers, many in part-time or temporary roles, earned an average of 2.11 million won ($1,589) a month from June through August, compared with 4.05 million won for regular employees. The resulting monthly pay gap of 1.94 million won was also a record. These figures describe a labor market expanding at its margins while offering too few paths into its protected core. The wage gap, however, needs careful interpretation. Monthly earnings do not account for differences in hours worked, and part-time roles make up a growing share of non-regular employment. Excluding part-time workers narrows the gap to 954,000 won. Even on this basis, a substantial disparity remains, pointing to disadvantages beyond shorter working hours. The shift also reflects Korea’s aging population. The number of non-regular workers aged 60 and older rose by 135,000, exceeding the overall increase of 103,000 as numbers fell in other age groups. Many work in health and social welfare, where non-regular employment grew by 112,000 over the year. Such jobs provide income and meet genuine care needs, but their expansion cannot compensate for a labor market in which younger workers struggle to establish lasting careers. The consequences can persist long after a first job ends. A study tracking 2,000 people born from 1989 to 1998 found that those who began in regular employment spent an average of eight years and three months in regular, full-time work over the following decade. Those who started in non-regular jobs accumulated just three years and two months. The difference in time spent unemployed was also two years. An insecure start can shape a working life for years to come. Employers have their own reasons to favor flexibility. At Korea’s five major banks, regular staffing fell by 4,080 between the end of 2022 and July 2026, while the non-regular headcount rose by 1,048. Digitization and branch closures have reduced demand for some conventional roles, giving banks further incentives to contain labor costs. Yet replacing experienced employees with a shifting pool of contractors can weaken institutional memory and make oversight harder. Payroll savings can come at the cost of service quality and internal controls. The government plans to publish a roadmap by year-end for equal pay for work of equal value. Beginning in 2027, it also plans to pay a “fairness allowance” to short-term public-sector contract workers upon departure. The aim of closing unjustified pay gaps is laudable. But a mandate alone cannot erase the incentives created by a system in which dismissal is difficult and wages often rise automatically with seniority. Employers may respond by slowing recruitment or outsourcing more work. Younger workers could end up bearing the cost of reforms intended to help them. Pay should reflect the work performed rather than years spent in a post, with employers given reasonable room to reorganize and workers protected by portable social benefits when jobs end. A labor market that protects those already inside while restricting entry for everyone else will struggle to turn economic growth into broad-based opportunity. Equal pay will remain an empty promise if access to secure employment continues to narrow.
